items.title: Tillis Knifes Controversial Trump Nominee for GAO
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Time Is Running Out on the Ueland Nom

Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) appears poised to effectively kill the nomination of White House aide Eric Ueland to a 15-year term as head of the Government Accountability Office.

Overnight, Tillis told Politico that he will block the Ueland nomination from being included in a package of presidential nominations the Senate will vote to confirm next month before the clock runs out on the GOP majority.

“I’ve already issued a presumptive hold if it comes out of committee,” Tillis said in an interview last night. “I won’t allow him to go through en bloc.”

The showdown over the lame-duck attempt to install Ueland as comptroller general of the United States has pitted a White House testing the new limits of its powers after a midterm shellacking against a shell-shocked GOP-controlled Senate that has endured two years of Trump humiliations and encroachments on its power. (Democrats in the minority are mostly bystanders to this mini-saga, though they have stirred the pot to the extent possible.)

Ueland’s nomination was like throwing gas on a smoldering fire. He is the deputy director of the White House Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the radical who spearheaded Trump’s Project 2025 agenda. No one more than Vought has sought to erode Congress’ Article I powers and vest them in the executive branch. No one has done more to bypass, repudiate, and weaken Congress’ power of the purse.

Under the circumstances, putting Ueland in charge of the GAO was a fox-guarding-the-henhouse move. Vought’s OMB has been engaged in a running gun battle with the GAO over the Impoundment Control Act, which only the comptroller general can sue to enforce. The nomination of Ueland was a thumb in the eye of Republicans to see how much more abuse they’d willingly take from Trump even after he cost them their majorities in both chambers.

It also highlighted the structural flaw of having the GAO serve as a creature of the legislative branch, but with its head appointed by the president. The White House had stonewalled the nominating of a new comptroller general for months, only to pivot to Ueland this week in a last-minute post-election move that left no time for consultation or vetting by the 10-member bipartisan, bicameral congressional commission that recommends candidates to the White House.

Senate rules are often the enemy of clarity, making it hard to declare outright that the Ueland nomination is dead. But Tillis’ move to block the nomination at this phase creates two difficult to surmount obstacles: It leaves little time for Republicans to get the nomination through on its own, and it robs Ueland of the protection of being in a package that senators have to take or leave as a whole.

There’s also no real reason to think Tillis — who didn’t seek re-election because he was almost certain to lose in the GOP primary without Trump’s support — wouldn’t put a hold on the nomination again if it came back up on its own. This appears to have been the easiest and quickest way for Tillis to knife the nomination for good but stay tuned.

WATCH: The Three Horseman of the Trump II Apocalypse

Almost exactly two years ago, just after the 2024 election, I wrote a post on “The Three Horsemen Of The Trump II Apocalypse” that framed the central themes of the incoming presidency as retribution, corruption, and destruction.

I went on the TPM Social Club podcast to talk about how that framing has fared, this week’s debut of Unsanctioned, and whole bunch of other stuff. Give it a listen:

The Destruction: Ph.D. Edition

The overall number of new full-time doctoral students in the sciences at U.S. universities fell 10% in the first year of Trump II, according to a NYT analysis. Among top-tier research schools, the decline was 11%, and three-quarters of that decline was driven by plummeting enrollment among international students.

The Retribution: Mar-a-Lago Edition

Bloomberg: “The Justice Department has deployed top Los Angeles prosecutor Bill Essayli to Miami for a special assignment to try probing the people involved in searching Trump’s Mar-a-Lago residence in 2022, said three people familiar with the situation.”

Jan. 6 Never Ends: Supercut Edition

BREAKING: Judge Blocks Trump Arch

U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema in Alexandria, Virginia, just issued an oral preliminary injunction from the bench against Trump’s triumphal arch.

Secretary Rollins Violated Constitution With Christmas and Easter Emails

A federal judge in California ruled yesterday that Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins violated the First Amendment’s Establishment Clause when she sent overtly religious Christmas and Easter emails to all department employees.

Great Read on Grand Theft Auto VI

I’m not now and never really have been a gamer, but I’ve been fascinated by the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. I know I’ve already lost a few of you, but there’s a great read coming here in a moment so hang in there.

Just to give fellow non-gamers some sense of the scale of the enterprise: GTA VI cost about $1.4 billion to develop and was projected to reach $3.3 billion in sales in its first week, according to the WSJ. Then on the first day of release yesterday, it hit an estimated $2.36 billion in sales, Reuters reports.

For a non-gamer like me trying to understand this as an entertainment business and cultural phenomenon, it was helpful to see the projected sales compared to more familiar events like the 2024 Olympics, Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour, and Hamilton Broadway sales :

Now to the fun part. Allowed pre-release access under an NDA, Joseph Bernstein has written a tour de force on GTA VI for the NYT Mag. I don’t want to spoil it for you, but if you want a super smart read that bridges the gap for non-gamers, I highly recommend it.

If you’re still not convinced, he describes the satirical elements of the game in a way that sounds like a post-apocalyptic virtual world that Barbara Ehrenreich would recognize, as if “Nickel and Dimed” married “Miami Vice” and gave birth to the Trump era. Enjoy!

items.title: Cornyn Nixes Judgeship for OLC Head After Shouting Match With Ted Cruz
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Author of Boat Strike Memo Is From Ohio

Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) appears to have killed the judicial nomination of T. Elliot Gaiser, the 37-year-old head of the Office of Legal Counsel at the Trump DOJ who authored legal justifications for some of the administration’s most egregious extralegal conduct, including the lawless boat strike campaign.

“He’s not from Texas. He hasn’t been vetted. And this is a lifetime job, and there’s better qualified people to hold that job,” Cornyn told the AP. “This is part, of course, of the constitutional responsibility of senators in the Senate to provide advice and consent. But it’s hard to provide advice and consent when there’s zero consultation, which happened in that case.”

Gaiser did not appear on the confirmation hearing yesterday for a batch of Trump judicial nominees (who as a group refused to say that the Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021). Cornyn’s leverage over the nomination comes from the Senate’s “blue-slip” tradition, still honored by Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Charles Grassley (R-IA), of not moving judicial nominations without the approval of home state senators.

Cornyn’s public break with the administration came after he and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) got into a loud argument on the Senate floor Tuesday over the Gaiser nomination. The whole imbroglio is heavily colored by Cornyn losing re-election in the GOP primary after Trump endorsed his opponent Ken Paxton, who went on to lose the general election that Cornyn his convinced he himself would have won.

Things continued to spill out in public on Wednesday with the Justice Department tacking a whack at Cornyn: “It is deeply disappointing that Senator Cornyn would choose political obstruction over advancing a highly qualified nominee.”

Cruz put out his own statement warning that there’s not time to confirm anyone else to the vacant judgeship: “If the Senate Judiciary Committee does not move Gaiser forward, the people of Texas will pay the price because it will effectively give the judicial seat to the Democrats, who will keep it vacant in perpetuity,” Cruz said. “That would be a tragedy.”

Another outgoing GOP senator primaried by President Trump got a measure of revenge.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA), the chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, abruptly cancelled a committee vote on the nomination of Jim O’Neill to lead the National Science Foundation.

O’Neill previously worked in multiple roles at the Department of Health and Human Services under Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements from Secretary Kennedy,” said Cassidy, who indicated that some other members of the committee shared his concerns.

Cassidy’s move effectively scuttled the nomination.

Election 2026 By the Numbers

A few new data points as the vote-counting nears an end:

  • Democrats lead in the national House vote has expanded to 14-percentage points, the largest margin by either party since Democrats romped by 16.6 points in the 1974 post-Watergate election.

  • Democrats have won at least 257 House seats, with six races still uncalled by the AP.

  • At least 109 House seats will be held by freshman, the most since at least 1998.

  • : Allies have launched Team Pete PAC to back another presidential run by the former secretary of transportation. (Politico)

  • : The Democratic senator from Arizona is bringing longtime aide Emma Brown back into the fold as he considers a White House run. (Politico)

  • : “Looking at it right now, it’s absolutely a savagely brutal map,” said Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-OH), the incoming chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee. (Politico)

The Dog That’s Obviously Not Barking

After the Trump DOJ brought a flurry of noncitizen voting cases right before the election — touting them with press releases, press conferences, and mug shots — it has brought only one new noncitizen voting case since the Nov. 3 election, the WaPo reports.

The Corruption: IRS Edition

ProPublica reports on under-the-radar Trump administration settlement of a claims against the IRS for leaking taxpayer info.

It recalls Trump’s own settlement with the IRS and the planned creation of $1.776 billion slush fund.

But it’s not Trump this time.

It’s the longtime golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley.

And despite the settlement, the case isn’t over yet.

Two other people connected to Trump properties are trying to get in on the action: a retired accountant at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley and a former lifeguard at the Trump golf club in Westchester County, New York.

  • Colorado Pubic Radio: In a new contempt of court ruling, U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney excoriated ICE for repeatedly violating court orders with its policy of immediately re-detaining immigrants after they had been ordered to be released from detention. But Sweeney declined to take any further action, ruling that ICE officials had cured the contempt of court by ceasing the practice at issue.

  • Greg Sargent: ICE has $91 billion of no-strings-attached funding to spend on deportations between now and the end of Trump’s second term.

  • Nicholas Kristof: Trump ‘Disappeared’ Them in 2025. I Found Them, Locked Up and Famished.

Bo French Booted From Country Club

Republican Bo French’s racist (and losing) campaign for Texas Railroad Commission has cost him his membership in the River Crest Country Club in Fort Worth. The country club’s board of directors booted him after he refused to resign his membership.

Thanks For All the AI Feedback!

I received quite a rich and varied response to my question yesterday about which AI tools you’ve found to be useful. Many thanks for taking the time to email.

First off, y’all are awesome. You’re a remarkable cross section of creatives and what we now call “knowledge workers” (I hate that term): scientists, engineers, teachers, musicians, writers, attorneys, CEOs, founders, environmental consultants, and IT experts — many of whom are also doing side gigs for fun. Those of you who purport to be retired are busy af, serving on boards and volunteering and running your own pet projects.

You’ve discovered uses for AI that range from the practical to the whimsical to the sublime. This initial sampling of reader responses are personal and side projects uses that delighted me:

TPM Reader : “I manage my own forested acreage in Washington State for enjoyment, health, and minor income. I was kind of at a point where I wanted to get more focused, more deliberate, and more comprehensive in my management planning and use of my time and labor. My son suggested I get a monthly ChatGPT account to facilitate that. The results have been dazzling.”

TPM Reader : “It helped me build two ten foot bird feeder poles with offset arms to stop raccoons and squirrels.”

TPM Reader : “Because of ChatGPT I have been able to do a pet project, a searchable index of historic cookbooks in the public domain.”

items.title: A Peek at What We Still Don’t Know About the Worst of Trump II … So Far
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Trump Sicced the IRS on Protesters

I hinted in yesterday’s Unsanctioned that one of the major benefits of Congress reviving its oversight powers under new Democratic majorities will be to provide a fuller accounting of what’s already happened in the first two years of Trump II.

As bad as it’s been on the retribution, corruption, and destruction fronts, we only know a fraction of what’s really gone down. Vigorous congressional oversight — absent under the GOP majorities — promises to gives us a clearer picture of the worst of the Trump II depredations, like the mass deportation operation, and uncover wrongdoing we don’t even know about yet.

We get a new peek today at what that might look like in a NYT story that shows the IRS directly involved in targeting left-wing political groups in the aftermath of the assassination of Charlie Kirk. The IRS “initiated at least four criminal investigations” into as-yet-unidentified left-wing groups, according to a portion of an internal memo obtained by the NYT.

“The memo describes the work done by a group of a dozen I.R.S. officials detailed to a task force formed in response to Mr. Kirk’s death on Sept. 10, 2025,” the NYT reports.

As TPM’s Josh Kovensky has reported at length, while the Trump administration ostentatiously turned Kirk’s death into a national day of mourning, it also seized on the assassination as a pretext to criminalize dissent, invent a left-wing terrorism threat that it falsely claimed had international connections, and scrutinize left-wing political and advocacy groups in an effort to intimidate and cow protests.

In the two weeks after Kirk’s death, President Trump designated Antifa as a terrorist organization and signed National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7). In NSPM-7, Trump ordered the IRS commissioner “to ensure that no tax-exempt entities are directly or indirectly financing political violence or domestic terrorism” and to refer such organizations and their officers and employees to the DOJ for investigation and prosecution.

“The memo viewed by The Times is the first window into the work the I.R.S. has actually undertaken to carry out the demands from the White House,” according to the story.

In March of this year, the IRS criminal investigations branch began working with the the task force that was operating out of the FBI headquarters, according to the NYT story. The memo covers work done between March and July. The NYT said it reviewed the first six pages of the eight-page memo. The last two pages, which the newspaper did not see, apparently identified the four targeted groups.

The protests at Delany Hall, the immigration detention center in Newark, New Jersey, have been a particular focus of the task force:

I.R.S. officials reviewed financial information, including subpoenaed Venmo records, about people arrested during those protests, as well as businesses that the officials believed could be funding them. At one point, I.R.S. officials used facial recognition and tattoo analysis databases to help identify individuals, the memo said.

A quick summary of some of the memo’s highlights, as reported by the NYT:

  • In addition to the Delaney Hall protests, the IRS also assisted in the response to the April shooting at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, the May shooting at a mosque in San Diego, and the June UFC event on the White House lawn. It’s not clear from the memo what role the IRS had in the UFC event (five men were charged with allegedly plotting to attack the event).

  • At least four tax-exempt groups were referred to the civil side of the agency, which conducts audits;

  • IRS officials have been assigned to nine grand juries.

The memo is just a glimpse into one discrete operation during one window of time this year, and it alone can’t really provide a clear picture of the scale and scope of the effort to turn political opposition to the Trump administration into criminal conduct. That’s one area where a Democratic Congress could bring new facts to light and begin to back the Trump administration off from its worst excesses.

President Trump brought an ignominious end to the political career of Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) by endorsing the scoundrel Ken Paxton and costing Texas a Senate seat — and now it’s having knock-on effects in the final weeks before Cornyn leaves office.

Cornyn appears to be very much on board with having Ohio native T. Elliot Gaiser — the head of the Trump DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel — installed as a federal judge in Texas, where he has few personal or professional connections.

A coveted federal judgeship going to a non-Texan while bypassing the home state senators’ approved list of potential nominees would be a tough ask by any president under any circumstance (unless you’re Ted Cruz, I guess). But under these circumstances, it’s a lot to expect Cornyn to roll over after getting royally screwed:

Cornyn’s remarks came as Bloomberg reported that last year, early in his tenure at OLC, Gaiser pitched a memo that proposed reviving the 1873 Comstock Act to criminalize the transportation of abortion drugs and related medical supplies.

Then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche rejected Gaiser’s pitch, according to Bloomberg’s sources: “Blanche pushed back by directing him to table the issue due to his worry that Gaiser’s position would amount to a federal abortion ban — an issue the administration had avoided wading into before the midterms …”

In an unusual move, Gaiser contacted Bloomberg directly after it published its story and denied it. “Your story is categorically false, period,” Gaiser said. “I did not push for any nationwide abortion ban.”

Where Have You Found AI Most Useful?

I ask this question with some trepidation. For a number of reasons, I have been slow to take affirmative steps to incorporate AI into my personal and professional lives.

I haven’t activated AI on my Apple devices or integrated it into Google yet. I’ve played around with Claude for maybe two hours over the past six months, and I used Gemini to create a couple of satirical images to make a friend laugh (with mixed results). I’ve not touched ChatGPT, and I haven’t used any of the new personal AI agents like Muse.

But I am curious about AI’s utility and how you’re incorporating it as a tool in your lives and work. I’m also pretty leery of the privacy risks involved — so I’d be interested in hearing where you’re drawing the line on entrusting AI tools with personal or sensitive information.

At this point, I should acknowledge that AI is a dreadfully imprecise term so let me refine what I mean for the purposes of this question. If you’re scientist, engineer, developer, or otherwise use AI at a high technical level, I’m probably not looking for for feedback from you. But even that can be a fuzzy line to draw. For example, a friend who is not a professional coder used AI to code a draftboard for his fantasy baseball team. So the newest AI tools may put some of what we used to think of as technical work within reach of a layperson. Obviously the AI I’m talking about here is a far cry from the frontier work on artificial general intelligence. You get the idea.

Let me try to preempt the emails warning me about the evils of AI or how you’re not using it and will never use it. I get you. My own slow adoption of AI is partly because it gives me pause, too. This has been a new frontier of consumer tech that I’ve been content not to be on the cutting edge of. But it’s pervasiveness at what I’ll call the retail level — quite apart from its role in research and development, core science, and other technical applications — has me prepared to adapt … possibly.

Thanks in advance for your feedback. My contact information is immediately below.

items.title: The Trump White House Can Run from Real Congressional Oversight But It Can’t Hide
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
As usual, there’s no one prism through which to see the upcoming fight over Democrats daring to conduct congressional oversight — but the best prism is that the Trump White House just wants to run out the clock until the end of his term.

Yes, it’s also fundamentally a continuation of the administration’s subordination of Congress in contravention of the constitutional order (except that it no longer has a supine GOP Congress to run over). It’s also an effort to save the administration’s political neck by blocking further revelations of corruption and wrongdoing. It’s also an attempt to project dominance and assert control at a time of acute political weakness.

But most of all, it’s an attempt to buy time.

The Trump administration is going to throw up an incredible amount of chaff to delay, obscure, and knock Democrats — but especially the political press — off track. It started with the absurd campaign to frame winning Democrats’ promises of congressional oversight as criminal threat. It continues with new Trump Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requiring that every government official and agency obtain White House approval before testifying before Congress. It will soon devolve into refusing to comply with congressional subpoenas, raising preposterous objections, and asserting flimsy claims of privilege, especially executive privilege.

We know what’s coming on that front. It’s clear as can be. And it will be an easy pissing match for the press to cover. But it’s not a winnable fight for congressional Democrats: They can’t prevail in court in the 18 months they have to engage in the fight. Plus, the fight itself doesn’t really tell an especially compelling political story that serves the public interest or their own political interest.

When viewed in that light, the initial inclination is to figure out how congressional Dems can speed things up and prevent the administration from simply stonewalling until its time in office is up. But at a practical level there are probably only marginal gains to be had on speed, mainly in not dilly dallying before launching the first waves of oversight. Pursuing unwinnable fights would be frustrating and demoralizing.

So if you can’t speed it up, then what to do?

The more practical approach for the Democratic Congress is to be very clear about what it aims to achieve with oversight, realistic about what is possible, and relentless in pursuing those aims in every available way. (They should still push for maximum speed and take the administration to court to keep the pressure on and eventually, maybe with a different Supreme Court, reassert its authority within the constitutional order. But that should be seen as a necessary line of attack — but not centered as the primary one.)

The primary lines of attack should be the ones that best tell a story of the retribution, corruption, and destruction of the Trump II presidency — and which can be told without overly relying on the tools of congressional oversight that are going to be the least useful to the purpose: subpoenas of the Trump administration and hauling in Trump officials for public hearings.

The Trump White House is eager for opportunities to confront Congress over process and procedure, like resisting subpoenas. It will savor chances like public hearings to confront elected Democrats directly and defy them in public with absurd behavior that rejects the very premise of congressional oversight. It’s all drearily predictable. So there’s no reason for Democrats in Congress to play that game unless and until it suits their broader aims in particular circumstances. Pick your spots.

That still leaves a lot of room for congressional oversight that can have real impact, and there are some signs that Democrats get this. A sample, non-comprehensive list includes:

: A premium source of unsanctioned disclosures for congressional investigators will be whistleblowers inside and outside of government. It will includes current government employees, former government officials in the first two years of Trump II, and federal contractors and grant recipients. All of these categories of whistleblowers have protections under the law for divulging corruption and wrongdoing, including retaliation against them. They have first-hand accounts and in some instances documentary evidence that doesn’t need to be subpoenaed or otherwise pried loose from the administration.

Government contractors and grant recipients: Congress can subpoena the companies, organizations, and other entities that the federal government does business with, thereby bypassing the administration. Congressional investigators have a potentially rich trove of documents and witnesses to mine here. The list is too long to do it justice, but to give you a sampling it includes everyone from defense contractors to NGOs crippled by the USAID cuts to construction companies working on Trump’s pet projects to ICE vendors. It includes not just prime contractors but subcontractors, suppliers, and vendors.

: Congressional investigations can legitimately reach beyond the federal government and the companies that directly do business with it to those people and entities who have been targeted by the Trump administration, who have capitulated, and who have curried favor with it. This category is also too broad to fully list here but think along the lines of: the Big Law firms and media companies who negotiated settlements with Trump; the donors to the Trump ballroom project and the Trump library; the research centers where grants and funding have been cut or politicized or both; the universities ostensibly targeted for alleged anti-semitism or for allegedly continuing affirmative action in admissions; industries crippled by illegal tariffs, etc.

It is, as the military would say, a target-rich environment. Democrats can make retribution, corruption, and destruction the storyline themselves or use those as the underpinnings for broader stories about affordability or whatever other line of attack they see as more accessible or voter-friendly.

None of this is easy, but it’s all very doable, and they’re are plenty of signs that Democrats already recognize the opportunities here. One of the real advantages to controlling both chambers is the power of agenda-setting: You can pick which stories to tell and which not to. You have flexibility to pivot as new information emerges or as public sentiment coalesces or shifts.

I wanted to frame this all up for you in part to set expectations. I wouldn’t be looking to the courts for salvation on congressional oversight, at least not in the next 18 months. I wouldn’t expect the Trump administration to do anything that even implicitly recognizes the legitimacy of the Democratic Congress. If you’re most desired endgame is Stephen Miller in tears at the witness table in an ornate Senate hearing room, let it go.

The hard work of congressional oversight is mostly away from the cameras doing due diligence and painstakingly reviewing documents and databases. The magic — which few investigators and electeds have the skillsets to pull off — is in being able to convert that hard work into politically salient storylines that resonate in the public consciousness.

It doesn’t necessarily have to be a Watergate or Jan. 6 hearing or other mega-scandal to break through. It can be done with less celebrated stories, and often it’s not the story you expected or foresaw. Facts are funny that way. They sometimes capture the public imagination in surprising and unanticipated ways.

While it’s true that President Trump’s corrupt decimation of the Justice Department deprives congressional Democrats (and us all) of enforcement mechanisms for contempt of Congress and of criminal and civil accountability for wrongdoing, congressional oversight has not lost its salience.

Perhaps the most powerful effect of congressional oversight is that it’s — to borrow another military phrase — a force multiplier. The fruits of congressional investigations combine with good journalism, ongoing legal proceedings, state and investigations to reinforce and buttress each other. Each can leverage the other to unearth new facts, puts those facts in proper context, and shine a concentrated light on wrongdoing and wrongdoers. It’s a powerful combination.

Politico’s Alice Ollstein: Georgia, Kansas and Texas eye Medicaid expansion after midterms romp

Cornyn Signals Trouble For OLC Head

Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) is poised to sink President Trump’s judicial nomination of T. Elliot Gaiser — who as head of the DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel has sanctioned some of the worst depredations of the Trump II presidency.

Gaiser’s confirmation hearing was set for this morning, but Cornyn signaled yesterday that he may not yield on the Gaiser nomination to a federal judgeship in Texas.

Under the Senate’s blue-slip tradition, Cornyn’s approval would be typically be required to move the nomination. Gaiser, an Ohion native, has very limited connections to Texas and was not on the short list that the two Texas senators sent to the White House.

For the second time this year, President Trump told a Black female journalist that she doesn’t “see dirt.”

Trump’s comments yesterday came in response to a question from NBC White House correspondent Yamiche Alcindor, who is Black:

Back in May, Trump made a virtually identical comment in response to a question from ABC News senior political correspondent Rachel Scott, who is also Black. “You probably don’t see dirt,” he said, gesturing to Scott. “But I do.”

items.title: Let Trump Own Every Bit of the Disasters He’s Created
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
This is the first edition of Unsanctioned, the weekday newsletter formerly known as Morning Memo. Unsanctioned will continue chronicling the historic threats and deep absurdities of the late-stage Trump era.

For longtime readers, I explained last week what will change and what will remain the same from its predecessor Morning Memo. New readers who want to receive Unsanctioned via email can sign up for free.

I’m glad you’re all here. Let’s get to it.

Setting the Post-Election Scene

We’re in a particularly weird interregnum between the historic midterm elections and the new Democratic-controlled Congress taking power in January — but get used to it because much of the weirdness is likely to persist through the 2028 election.

With an erratic lame-duck GOP president largely insulated from the political winds of the moment but eager to wield his veto power, the next two years on the Hill are going to be largely about containing him and mitigating further damage. The remaining balance of the political and legislative work will be spent on setting the stage for winning a Democratic trifecta in 2028, at which point the real work of undoing the worst of the Trump II damage and getting the country back on track can begin.

But as the events of the last few days showed with remarkable clarity, the world continues to spin in accelerated fashion thanks to Trump II. Whether it’s a nationwide FAA outage (thoughts with readers stranded over the weekend), a high-flying AI CEO brought low by a honeypot, the threats of climate change, or the revocation of the U.S.’s measles elimination status, events aren’t going to wait until the United States gets its politics sorted and shores up its democracy.

Expectations among Democratic partisans continue to be way out of whack given the limitations of even hefty majorities in both chambers — expectations only exceeded by the chronic hand-wringing that elected Democrats are going to screw it all up and squander the opportunity.

Foremost among the misplaced expectations is that Democrats should project some main character energy so that we can finally shuffle the narcissistic president off his mark at center stage. But absent the ravages of old age taking a sudden and unexpected toll, Trump isn’t going anywhere for the next two years — and the Constitution does, for better or worse, vest main character energy in the president. Given the current economic and political landscape, that’s just fine.

Why would Democrats willingly shoulder the yoke of cleaning up Trump’s colossal mess when they didn’t create it and don’t yet have the power to fix it?

Be skeptical anytime anyone says Democrats “must” do this or “have to” do that. Democrats have maximum flexibility and maneuvering room for the next year and half. They’re not bound to do any one thing, including rescuing Trump from himself. They can do everything or nothing. They can pick and choose. They can leave Trump dangling in the wind.

Don’t let Trump off the hook by overstating Democrats’ power to rein him in. He is an ongoing disaster, and voters saw it clearly for what it was. He will spend the next two years flailing just as spectacularly — while Democratic oversight will likely uncover new and even more dire examples of the disaster that was the last two years. Republicans in competitive races in 2028 — including the presidential candidates — will be trapped looking for any way to simultaneously run away from Trump and shift the blame to Democrats for the Trump catastrophe. It’s a very strong position for Democrats to be in.

Brian Beutler: “A new project, spearheaded by veterans of the Obama and Biden administrations, should hearten those of us who are concerned the Democratic Party will return to power in 2029 unprepared to build a functioning government atop the wreckage of the Trump regime.”

“I don’t think we should play this game where the things we want have to be paid for and the things they want can be put on a credit card. So I’m cautious about falling into that trap, but if we can find pay-fors, that’s even better.”—Sen. Brian Schatz (D-HI), confronting the long-running double standard that the GOP can spend like drunken sailors when in power while Democrats must exercise fiscal restraint when they win

  • : At the last minute, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a temporary restraining order late Saturday blocking the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park in D.C. as scheduled on Sunday. But she stopped short of ordering the administration to keep the East Potomac Golf Course in operation — and it has now shut down. Trump has vowed to appeal.

  • : Anna Bower on the new revelations about how far the Trump DOJ has been willing to go to vindictively prosecute former FBI Director James Comey

  • : Marcy Wheeler on the DOJ’s ploy to keep line prosecutors off the stand as U.S. District Judge April Perry investigates potential contempt of court

Must Read on Boat Strikes

WaPo: “A high-tech surveillance plane that repeatedly flew in the vicinity of CIA-linked attacks on boats near the Galápagos Islands this year had an unlikely first owner: a company based in The Villages, the retirement mega-community in Florida.”

What a Difference Two Years Make

At this point in 2024, Reps. Lauren Boebert (R-CO), Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-GA), and Rep. Matt Gaetz (R-FL) had just been re-elected to Congress, and Gaetz was President Trump’s announced pick for attorney general.

Within weeks, Gaetz wasn’t just out of the running for attorney general, he resigned his seat and was out of Congress. Greene likewise resigned, earlier this year. And with Boebert’s defeat in this year’s election now official, the entire MAGA squad will be gone come January.

items.title: Why the Trump DOJ Is More of a Wreck Than Ever
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
A lot of things happened. Here are some of the things. This is TPM’s Morning Memo.

A Two-Tiered Justice Department

Before jumping into the news, I wanted to frame up quickly how to think about the current structure of the Justice Department as we head into the second half of Trump II.

The departures of some top political appointees from the Trump DOJ since the GOP was blown out in the midterms has gotten a lot of attention, but it’s been variously miscast, misunderstood, or mischaracterized.

The way the Justice Department historically worked was similar to every other department: A slate of political appointees was layered on top of the career employees to run the department and implement the president’s broad policy agenda. Those political appointees varied in terms of skill, professionalism, experience, and willingness to be independent versus do the White House’s bidding.

There were outliers — like Attorneys General John Mitchell and Bill Barr — but for the most part, the political appointees could be placed within a range that we might call “normal.” Then along came Trump II, and everything changed.

Attorneys General Pam Bondi and Todd Blanche exist far outside the normal range and have redefined what outliers are. They obliterated DOJ independence and participated in using the department as a sword against Trump’s foes and a shield for his friends.

They each surrounded themselves with a cadre of like-minded political appointees, but that circle is smaller than usual and has been getting steadily smaller. At this point, it’s down to Blanche, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, Associate Attorney General Stan Woodward, and Aakash Singh, the principal associate deputy attorney general. A former DOJer joked to the NYT that the Trump DOJ should be called “Four Guys” — a play on the burger chain’s name — to reflect its tiny leadership cadre.

Unlike past administration’s, the Trump II political appointees aren’t layered on top of the career employees in normal hierarchal fashion. They exist outside of that framework and in a posture not just adversarial to career employees but to some of the core functions of the department under the law, like public corruption and civil rights.

After the extensive Trump II purges of career employee, the political appointees now oversee a department Swiss-cheesed with a lack of capacity, abandoned units and sections, and absentee management. The only thing that keeps the department running in any recognizable form is that most of the day-to-day functioning of the DOJ happens in the 94 U.S attorney’s offices around the country. But they haven’t been spared either.

The rush for the exits among some political appointees post-election hasn’t really changed the core dynamic; it just more clearly reflects what was already going on. The department was already being run by the relative few remaining Trump true believers.

So small were there numbers and so preposterous their legal arguments that it’s been left to senior political appointees like Woodward to actually handle cases themselves, appearing in court, and earning the direct ire of federal judges. Woodward is defending inquiries in separate cases in D.C. and Chicago into whether the DOJ misled courts, and Woodward himself has come under withering criticism from judges.

The post-election departures have probably zapped some of the manpower that the political appointees have to handle cases directly themselves, although they’ve already shuffled in new attorneys to help. That’s a separate issue from the purges of career employees leaving DOJ beleaguered and under staffed, especially as it contends with a wave of immigrant habeas cases.

So when Singh — the conduit between Main Justice and the 94 U.S. attorneys — warned them after the election of firings to come and urged them to be on a “wartime footing,” it looked less like a powerful threat and more like flailing from a position of weakness.

While weakened, the Trump DOJ is no less dangerous after the election because it’s probably even more dysfunctional, unpredictable, and subordinate to the Trump White House.

Trump DOJ Sanctions Alert

A federal judge in the Eastern District of New York this week barred a Trump DOJ attorney from ever again appearing in a particular immigration case in front of him, Just Security reports. Two other DOJ attorneys in the case may suffer the same fate, the judge warned.

U.S. District Judge Sanket J. Bulsara said that a letter to the court from Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas Price was in “bad faith, a deliberate attempt to mislead the Court, perpetuate a fraud on the tribunal, and violate[s] obligations under Rule 11.”

The breach appears fatal to Price’s standing with the judge:

Judge Bulsara told Richard Hayes, head of the civil division at the U.S. Attorney’s office, that he should consider removing Price from other cases. “You should think about whether you want to swap him out and have some other lawyer from your office appear in any of his cases before me,” Judge Bulsara warned. “Your office is on notice.”

U.S. Attorneys Scheme: WDVA Edition

A criminal defendant is trying to disqualify Robert Tracci from acting as the top federal prosecutor in the Western District of Virginia, Bloomberg reports. Tracci’s appointment as first assistant U.S. Attorney came after the U.S. attorney position was already vacant, a circumstance which other courts have found insufficient to lawfully elevate the first assistant into the top post. It is one of the mechanisms that the Trump DOJ has used in its scheme to install loyalists as top federal prosecutors in blue states.

Stephen Miller Will Fail ‘Catastrophically’

Miles Taylor: “I spent the better part of two-and-a-half years dealing with Stephen Miller almost every day. And his selection [as White House chief of staff] is among the most dangerous, foolish, and self-defeating actions we’ve ever seen an American president take.”

Golf Course Case Heats Up

Ahead of a very contentious hearing this morning in the D.C. golf course case, the Trump DOJ told U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes that it objects to her plan to appoint a special master in the case. Reyes intends to have former D.C. U.S. Attorney Jessie Liu investigate whether the Trump DOJ or other government counsel misled the court in the case as a precursor to a potential contempt of court inquiry.

The hearing this morning started HOT — even though the hearing was ostensibly not about either the special master appointment or the DOJ’s alleged misconduct in the case. The immediate issue is that President Trump has ordered the closure of most of East Potomac Park, including the golf course, on Nov. 15, and the National Park Service plans to follow that direction. Plaintiffs are seeking a TRO to keep the park open.

Tying Up Some Loose Ends on the Election

: “In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald Trump to try to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election,” ProPublica reports.

The Big Lie of Noncitizen Voting: A federal magistrate judge in Wisconsin last week dismissed two voter fraud cases brought by the Trump DOJ. In each instance, the judge adopted a similar reasoning to a federal judge in Florida in a ruling last month. The gist is that the 40-year-old federal ban on noncitizen voting is unconstitutional because the states alone have the power to set voter qualifications in federal elections. The Florida case is on appeal, and there’s a lot more litigation coming over this. But it represents a big threat to Trump’s Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting.

Politico: DHS messages back up allegations that Lewandowski operated as shadow secretary

NYT: “A Mexican former prosecutor facing arrest after allowing Central Intelligence Agency officers to operate in his state has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.”

Next Week: Changes to Morning Memo

Tomorrow will mark four years since I took over writing Morning Memo. I assigned myself the task on what I thought would be a temporary basis until I found someone else to do it. It didn’t work out the way I expected.

That temporary fill-in ended up being the beginning of one of the most rewarding phases of my time here at TPM. At that point, I hadn’t written regularly in more than a decade, and I discovered how much I enjoyed the chance to do something directly myself rather than overseeing the doing of it by others.

Since then my role at TPM has evolved and so has the role of Morning Memo. Those changes accelerated in the first half of 2025 as we sailed into the teeth of the Trump II storm. Given the significance of the historical moment, Morning Memo gradually moved away from being a one-stop shop for all of the day’s essential political news and became instead a chronicle of the depredations of the Trump II presidency, with a special focus on the rule of law.

You may have also noticed the publishing time moved back closer to midday as the emphasis of Morning Memo changed from a rundown of the news to developing a taxonomy for and a shared narrative of the budding authoritarianism in America.

It became clear well before the election that it was time to repackage Morning Memo to better reflect what it has become. With the election past us, now’s the time to make the change. Beginning next week, “Morning Memo” will be renamed and its promise to you refined and updated.

Please welcome “Unsanctioned.”

I’ll be writing Unsanctioned every weekday. The substance of it will look very much like the Morning Memo of the past 22 months (which looked a bit different than the pre-Trump II version of Morning Memo that we started with). It will be repackaged and rebranded to reflect the new name and the new emphasis.

Among the changes, Unsanctioned will also offer extras exclusively to TPM members. It might be an extra edition on a busy news weekend or holiday. It might be a deeper dive on a topic or story than there’s room for in the standard version of Unsanctioned. It might be access to live interviews, additional news items, special news alerts, and other ways of serving you news and analysis.

If you were already receiving Morning Memo via email, you don’t need to do a thing to receive Unsanctioned. It will pop up in your inbox starting next week. If you have liked Morning Memo, you’ll feel right at home with Unsanctioned. And while I want to provide TPM members with additional ways to connect with Unsanctioned, non-members will still have access to what you’ve come to expect from me each weekday.

I’m looking forward to embarking together with you on this next phase for the country and for what I do here at TPM. I’m excited by the possibilities.

items.title: Donald Trump Will Do Anything to Get Ilhan Omar
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
A lot of things happened. Here are some of the things. This is TPM’s Morning Memo.

The Retribution: Somalia Edition

All of the discussion of the Trump White House’s resistance to oversight from the new Democratic Congress seems almost quaint in the context of the Trump DOJ raiding the home of a sitting Democratic member of Congress days before the election.

In a new development on that front, the NYT reports that the Trump administration took the unusual step of indicting one of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s former bodyguards in April for a felony related to his green card application in an attempt to flip him against her:

Mr. Mohamed’s lawyer, Bruce Rivers, said that prosecutors spent months trying to turn the bodyguard into an informant to bolster their case against Ms. Omar. In a move he described as shocking, Mr. Rivers said that prosecutors repeatedly told him and Mr. Mohamed that the investigation into Ms. Omar was “100 percent being run by 1600 Pennsylvania Ave.,” the address of the White House.

“I’ve never seen anything like this in my almost 28 years practicing law in federal court,” said Mr. Rivers, a veteran criminal defense lawyer in Minneapolis.

The case was by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Minnesota, but as the NYT notes: “The government lawyers assigned to the case were early-career federal prosecutors who were promoted to leadership roles in the U.S. attorney’s office in Minneapolis after several veteran attorneys left the office early this year in protest over its handling of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota.”

As the NYT puts it, the Trump DOJ “failed” to flip the bodyguard, but he was offered immunity and was brought before a D.C. grand jury investigating the Minnesota Democrat, where he reportedly testified to having no substantive knowledge of Omar’s immigration and marriage history.

The next day the Trump DOJ moved to dismiss the indictment, with the explanation from prosecutors that the bodyguard was in removal proceedings: “Accordingly, there is no longer a federal interest in continuing prosecution in light of his anticipated removal from the United States.” Take that as you will.

Before the election, Greg Sargent and Brian Beutler spoke to a number of House and Senate Democrats and senior aides about whether they were prepared for the extreme resistance to congressional oversight that the Trump White House was expected to demonstrate. Their conclusion:

Every Democrat we spoke with agreed that the Trump administration is world-historically corrupt, and most expected his lawbreaking to persist or even escalate. Some do seem willing to contemplate suspension of the regular order of things, if that’s what it takes to slow or stop the lawlessness. Others, though, seem more resigned to running a playbook for normal times, one that’s plainly unsuited to the coming moment.

The Trump White House resistance is already manifesting in absurd claims that congressional oversight is itself criminal.

Rep. Jared Huffman (D-CA), the ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, is demanding that the Interior Department preserve documents related to President Trump’s pet construction projects around D.C., CNN reports:

Multiple credible whistleblowers have approached Huffman’s committee in recent weeks to voice concern that the Interior Department is getting rid of records in anticipation of forthcoming scrutiny, the sources told CNN. The agency oversees much of the national parkland Trump wants to use for his projects.

The Interior Department called the whistleblower claims “100% false.”

Josh Marshall: Understanding the Scandal/Accountability Conveyor Belt

Still Basking in the Election Aftermath

A sampling of election news:

  • : Not a single Democratic incumbent in the House lost in the general election, the WaPo notes.

  • : Rep. Mike Turner (R-OH), who was swept out of office by the blue wave after nearly a quarter of a century in the House, blames his loss on that controversial ad by GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy: “That final ad from Vivek really was kind of a lightning strike at the end, and it had an impact up and down the ticket in all the races … Absolutely that was the margin at the end.”

  • : Democrats are one uncalled state Senate election away from having a trifecta in North Carolina. But in that very close race, state Sen. Danny Britt (R) still leads Catina Hamm (D) by 228 votes even though the race has tightened since election night. The race remains within the margin for a recount.

After all three levels of the federal courts blocked its lawsuit seeking to use the Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting to interfere in the California election, the Trump DOJ moved to dismiss the case with a pissy filing complaining about all that losing.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter granted the dismissal, but not without taking a parting shot at the administration:

This lawsuit attempted to disrupt an ongoing election and create confusion and uncertainty for voters and election workers alike. The right to vote is sacred. So, too, is trust in our democracy. Upon recent receipt of the Department of Justice’s unilateral withdrawal of its Complaint in its entirety, and pursuant to the Department’s request, the expedited hearing this Court set regarding the validity of the government’s list for Friday, November 13, 2026 is now and hereby vacated. In light of the government’s withdrawal, this case is .

  • Fatal ICE Shooting in Maine: The ICE officer involved in a fatal shooting of a Colombia national in Maine over the summer previously expressed hatred of immigrants — especially Colombians — castigating his sister for her longtime relationship with a Colombian man, with whom she had two children, the NYT reports.

  • : Kim Wehle on how ICE is making immigrants vanish from its system.

  • : An ICE deportation carrying Iranian nationals to Pakistan, where they were to be handed over to Iran, turned around midair and landed back in Arizona after Pakistan refused to accept the detainees, sources tell the NYT.

What the Iran War Has Unleashed

  • In a new superseding indictment this week, federal prosecutors alleged that Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a leader of an Iranian-backed militia, passed along coded messages from jail in Brooklyn that were delivered to operatives working on behalf of Iran to target the Royal Air Force base at Fairford. In response to the alleged plot, the U.S. evacuated its military aircraft from the base last month.

  • In response to alleged Iranian threats against his life, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently moved out of his D.C. home and onto an unspecified nearby military base, the NYT reports.

One day after avoiding impeachment in the House, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth beclowned himself at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier:

Jensen Huang and Over-Concentration

Before Jensen Huang resigned this morning as the CEO of Nvidia, economist Justin Wolfers had used the scandal to show the dangerous concentration of power in one man at one company in one sector of the economy. It is parallel to (and overlapping with) the over-concentration of power in Donald Trump.
